blocks.text: CHOSEN: THE STORY BEFORE THE MANGER
SCENE 9 — “WHAT WILL HE BE?” / THE TOWN TURNS
Musical Number: “What Will He Be?” — approximately 2–2½ minutes
Mary and Joseph are walking home together.
The familiar sound of Nazareth begins before the marketplace is fully visible.
The same work vocabulary from Scene 1.
The same stalls. The same baskets. The same fabric. The same people.
For a breath, it feels like home.
Mary and Joseph enter at the edge of the marketplace, still holding hands.
No one has become a villain. They simply know—or think they know.
Mary feels the change in the room before anyone says anything.
Nia runs toward her before an adult can stop her.
Simon follows, more cautiously. Several children trail behind.
Simon looks at Mary. Then Joseph. Then Mary again.
You cannot just ask people things like that.
I was going to ask better.
Mary cannot help a small laugh.
Are you really having a baby?
Mary looks briefly at Joseph, then back to the children.
No scandal. No hesitation. Just a baby.
Babies do not tell you that.
You didn’t even know where babies—
A few adults react. Mary covers another laugh. Joseph does too.
Joseph is caught off guard—not by the question, but by the future inside it.
This time he does not avoid the answer.
If he wants to learn, I’ll teach him.
What if he’s terrible at it?
What do you think he’ll be?
The children lead. Warm, playful, imaginative. The number is entirely about possibility.
The adults remain in the marketplace, some working, some watching, some whispering.
The song must not explain who Jesus becomes. The audience supplies that knowledge.
Will he laugh too loud? / Will he sleep all day?
Will he race through every market stall / and leave his things in everybody’s way?
Will he ask a hundred questions / before anyone can breathe?
What will he be? What will he be?
When he is born, for all to see?
Will he be different or the same?
Will the whole world know his name?
What will he be? What will he be?
The children imagine ordinary futures: animals, stories, running, helping, learning, teaching, courage, kindness.
Will he build things out of wood?
Make a chair that’s strong and good?
Joseph looks at the child, then at Mary.
Will he like to run and play?
Help a friend along the way?
Will he dance and flip about?
Will he laugh and scream and shout?
What will he be? What will he be?
When he is born, for all to see?
Will he be different or the same?
Will the whole world know his name?
What will he be? What will he be?
When he is born, for all to see?
Will he be different or the same?
Will the whole world know his name?
Then why is he still with her?
She says there was an angel.
When he is born, for all to see?
Will he be different or the same?
Will the whole world know his name?
What will he be? (all together, kids laughing)
A brief release—then an adult voice.
Another adult calls a child away.
One by one, the children are removed from Mary’s orbit.
Mary watches a child who was laughing beside her moments ago get pulled away.
That hurts more than an insult.
A restrained fragment of “Welcome to Nazareth” lives underneath the dialogue, not celebratory now, but tight and repetitive.
In Scene 1, everybody knowing everybody was comedy.
Now everybody thinks they know enough.
She is not completely all right.
Adina joins them, scanning the marketplace.
I’m not trying to be helpful. I’m trying to be accurate.
A small breath of humor. Then—
The question is aimed at Talia.
Talia does not pretend certainty she does not have.
I believe Mary told us what happened to her.
That is not what I asked.
So you don’t believe it either.
Talia steps slightly closer to Mary.
Which means neither of us gets to humiliate her over something we did not see.
Levi, Malachi, Caleb, and Ezra enter or emerge from the marketplace.
They see the crowd. Then Joseph. Then Mary holding Joseph’s hand.
But I know enough to know she told me the truth.
This is me telling you what I chose.
Levi does not like it. But he hears him.
Caleb nods and moves to Joseph’s side.
There are still several things about this that make absolutely no sense.
Joseph almost smiles at the absurdity.
Ezra did not expect that either.
But understanding everything and knowing what I need to do are not always the same thing.
A Villager Man steps forward. Not a villain. A neighbor who believes he is saying the obvious thing.
Joseph. You don’t have to do this.
You don’t know what you’re talking about.
The Villager Man looks at him.
And you’re willing to throw away your name for this?
My name isn’t worth much if I have to destroy hers to protect it.
The Villager Man turns toward Mary.
Joseph does not step in front of Mary.
Some villagers stare. A few whisper. One or two may laugh under their breath.
And you expect all of us to believe that?
Mary looks around at people she has known all her life.
I can’t make you believe me.
But I will not call what happened to me a lie just to make you comfortable.
You don’t have to answer everyone.
But you can’t build your way out of this.
For once, he lets the problem remain unsolved.
Nia and Simon have watched all of this from nearby.
Mary gives her a small reassuring smile.
The ensemble reorganizes without becoming a cartoon of good people and bad people.
Near Mary and Joseph: Shira, Adina, Dafna, Talia, Caleb, Malachi, and Ezra.
At a distance: skeptical villagers, whisperers, people who simply do not know what to think.
Levi remains between the two groups.
The gossip rhythm begins to peak.
A Roman drum cuts through the marketplace.
A trumpet or unmistakable imperial sound.
Rome does not care about Nazareth’s scandal.
The Roman Announcer enters as though his arrival is unquestionably the most important event of the day.
A few villagers are still murmuring.
The Announcer stops and looks directly at them.
We haven’t even heard it yet.
A census shall be taken. Every household is to be registered according to family line and ancestral city.
If your ancestral city is elsewhere, yes.
You will present yourself, your household, and the required family information in the appropriate city.
Immediately! It is a wonderful word.
The marketplace explodes into practical anxiety: counting, packing, questions, arguments.
He begins to roll the decree.
He exits as the Roman drum resumes.
The marketplace is now moving for an entirely different reason.
He is doing the calculation before she asks.
Mary knows what that means: distance, travel, timing.
His first instinct is to protect her.
He sees that she is not asking whether she is going.
Their hands find each other again.
Around them, Nazareth prepares to move.
Scene 10 setup: Mary’s “When do we leave?” makes clear that the next conflict is not whether she will go, but how Joseph will handle the danger, logistics, and loss of control on the journey.

Scene 9 should feel like a deliberate mirror of Scene 1: same marketplace, same people, same work, even echoes of the same musical rhythm—but Mary and Joseph now experience that familiar community differently. The source is especially clear that Nazareth should become divided, not uniformly evil. Some people support them, some doubt them, some judge them, and others simply do not know what to think.
I’m also keeping Nia and Simon as our two child storytellers, but neither narrates this scene. Here, they are simply children of Nazareth experiencing what is happening alongside the other children.
The line I would especially protect for Mary is
MARY: “I can't make you believe me. But I will not call what happened to me a lie just to make you comfortable.”
That keeps her from becoming the passive person Joseph has to defend. Joseph protects her dignity publicly, but Mary owns her own truth.
JOSEPH: “My name isn't worth much if I have to destroy hers to protect it.”

is a direct reversal of the fear he admitted in Scene 8. Reputation mattered enormously to him; now he is publicly deciding that protecting Mary matters more. That is the public test the source specifically calls for.

And Talia should absolutely remain skeptical but stand beside Mary. That is more sophisticated than turning every friend into an instant believer. The source specifically distinguishes understanding Mary’s claim from refusing to participate in cruelty, and that gives Talia one of the strongest character payoffs among the friend group.

Finally, “What Will He Be?” should stay innocent. The children are wondering whether this child will be funny, brave, helpful, curious, or good with tools; the audience supplies the dramatic irony because they already know who He becomes. The song never needs to tell us.
